title: Intro to Personal Finance in South Africa
description: Budgeting, interest, credit scores and tax, in four commute-sized segments.

segments.title: A budget that survives month-end
segments.script: Most of us know roughly what we earn, but very few of us know where it goes. A budget is not a punishment. It is a plan for your money, so that your money does not make plans for you. Start with three numbers. First, your take-home pay, the amount that actually lands in your account after tax and UIF. Second, your fixed costs: rent, transport, airtime, debit orders, black tax, school fees. These do not move much from month to month. Third, everything else: groceries, data, weekends, the small things that add up. A simple rule to start with is fifty, thirty, twenty. Fifty percent of take-home pay goes to needs, thirty to wants, and twenty to saving or paying off debt. In South Africa, where a taxi to work and back can eat fifteen to twenty percent of a salary, your split will look different. The point is not the exact numbers. The point is that every rand has a job before the month starts. The most common mistake is budgeting for a perfect month. Real months have a funeral, a car problem, a cousin's wedding. So put a line in your budget called surprises, and give it something every month, even fifty rand. When the surprise comes, you have a place to take the money from that is not your rent. And before you change anything, track for one month. Use your bank app's transaction history. Do not guess. Most people find one or two categories that shock them, and that is where the first easy win is.
keyPoints: Three numbers: take-home pay, fixed costs, everything else
Track one real month before changing anything
segments.altExplanation: Think of your salary as a taxi full of passengers. Every rand is a passenger, and every passenger needs a destination before the taxi leaves the rank. Rent gets off first, then transport, then groceries. If you leave passengers with no destination, they get off wherever, usually at the Spur or the bottle store. The surprises line is the passenger you keep on board in case someone needs a lift to a funeral. Tracking a month is just checking where the passengers actually got off last time.
segments.deeper: The fifty thirty twenty split comes from a US book, and it assumes housing is around thirty percent of income. In many South African households transport plus housing is already over fifty percent, so a more honest local version is often sixty, twenty, twenty, or even seventy, twenty, ten. What matters is that the saving or debt slice is never zero. Stokvels are a budgeting tool many people already use without calling it that: a fixed monthly contribution that is socially hard to skip. If you are in one, count it as saving in your budget, and check whether the payout month lines up with your biggest annual expense, like school fees in January.

checkpoint.prompt: In the fifty thirty twenty rule, what does the twenty stand for?
checkpoint.rubric: Twenty percent goes to saving or paying off debt.

checkpoint.prompt: Why should a budget have a surprises line?
checkpoint.answer: Because real months have unplanned costs, and having money set aside means the surprise does not come out of essentials like rent.
checkpoint.rubric: Must mention that unexpected or unplanned costs happen AND that the line stops them coming out of essential money. Reject answers that only say 'to be safe' or 'for emergencies' with no reason.

segments.title: Interest works for you or against you
segments.script: Interest is the price of money over time. When you save, the bank pays you. When you borrow, you pay the bank. Same idea, pointing in opposite directions. Simple interest is calculated only on the original amount. Put one thousand rand in an account paying ten percent simple interest, and you earn one hundred rand every year. After three years you have one thousand three hundred. Compound interest is calculated on the original amount plus the interest you have already earned. Same one thousand rand at ten percent, compounded yearly. After year one you have one thousand one hundred. In year two you earn ten percent of one thousand one hundred, which is one hundred and ten, so now you have one thousand two hundred and ten. Year three takes you to one thousand three hundred and thirty one. The gap grows every single year. Over ten years the difference is over five hundred rand on that one thousand. Over thirty years it is thousands. This is why starting early matters more than starting big. A twenty-five year old saving five hundred rand a month will usually end up with more at sixty than a thirty-five year old saving a thousand a month, because the early money gets ten extra years of compounding. Now the flip side. Debt compounds too, just against you. Store cards and payday loans in South Africa can charge over twenty percent a year. Paying only the minimum on a store card means most of your payment goes to interest, and the balance barely moves. So if you have savings earning five percent and a store card charging twenty-two, paying off the card is the better return. You cannot find a savings account that beats twenty-two percent.
keyPoints: Simple interest: earned only on the original amount
Compound interest: earned on original plus interest already earned
Expensive debt compounds against you, so pay it before saving
segments.altExplanation: Picture a mielie field. Simple interest is planting the same ten seeds every season and eating the whole harvest. Compound interest is planting the ten seeds, then replanting part of every harvest, so each season the field is bigger than the last. The first few seasons look almost the same. By season ten the compound field is twice the size. Debt is the same field, except someone else is harvesting it and you are the one buying seeds.
segments.deeper: Banks quote a nominal annual rate but compound monthly or daily, which makes the effective rate slightly higher. A store card at twenty-two percent nominal compounded monthly is effectively about twenty-four percent a year. The National Credit Act caps interest on most consumer credit, but unsecured loans and credit cards can still legally charge over twenty percent, and short-term loans can be even higher once fees are included. The rule of seventy-two is a handy shortcut: divide seventy-two by the interest rate to get the years it takes money to double. At eight percent, savings double in nine years. At twenty-four percent, debt doubles in three.

checkpoint.prompt: One thousand rand at ten percent simple interest for three years gives you how much?
options: One thousand three hundred and thirty one
checkpoint.rubric: Simple interest earns one hundred each year, so one thousand three hundred after three years.

checkpoint.prompt: In your own words, why does compound interest grow faster than simple interest?
checkpoint.answer: Because each period's interest is calculated on the original amount plus the interest already earned, so the base keeps growing.
checkpoint.rubric: Must express that interest is earned on previously earned interest, or that the base amount grows each period. Reject 'because it compounds' or 'because it is more' with no mechanism.

checkpoint.prompt: You have five thousand rand in savings at five percent and a store card charging twenty-two percent. What should you do with the money?
checkpoint.answer: Pay off the store card, because the debt costs more than the savings earn.
checkpoint.rubric: Must say pay the card or the debt AND give the reason that the debt rate is higher than the savings rate. Reject answers that only say 'pay the debt' with no comparison.

segments.title: Your credit score follows you
segments.script: A credit score is a number, usually somewhere between zero and about seven hundred and fifty depending on the bureau, that summarises how reliably you have repaid money in the past. Lenders look at it. Landlords look at it. Sometimes employers look at it. In South Africa the main bureaus are TransUnion, Experian, and Compuscan, and you are entitled to one free credit report from each of them every year. So what builds a good score? Paying accounts on time, every time, even small ones like a cellphone contract. Keeping the amount you owe on a credit card well below the limit, ideally under thirty percent. And having a long history of accounts in good standing. What damages it? Missed payments. Accounts handed over to debt collectors. Judgments. And applying for lots of credit in a short time, because every application is recorded, and a burst of applications looks like someone in trouble. Two practical tips. First, if you have never borrowed, you have what is called a thin file, and lenders cannot see anything at all. A small cellphone contract or a clothing account, paid in full and on time every month, is a cheap way to build a history. Second, check your report once a year. Errors are common. And an account on your report that you never opened is a sign of fraud you want to catch early, not when you apply for a home loan.
keyPoints: Score summarises how reliably you have repaid money
Builds it: on-time payments, low card balance, long history
Damages it: missed payments, collections, many applications
One free report per bureau per year; check for errors
segments.altExplanation: Your credit score is like a reference from every landlord you have ever had, all rolled into one number. Pay on time and the reference says reliable. Miss payments and it says risky. Apply for ten places in one week and it says desperate. If you have never rented, there is no reference at all, which is almost as bad as a bad one. A small account paid perfectly is how you get your first good reference.
segments.deeper: Each bureau scores slightly differently, so your number will not match across TransUnion, Experian and Compuscan, but the direction will. Negative information stays on your report for a set time: missed payments for about two years, judgments for five, and a debt review flag until you receive a clearance certificate. Under the National Credit Act you can dispute an incorrect entry and the bureau must investigate within twenty business days. Prescribed debt is a related idea: most unsecured debt that has not been paid, acknowledged, or pursued in court for three years can no longer be legally collected, and it is illegal for collectors to pursue it.

checkpoint.prompt: How many free credit reports are you entitled to from each bureau per year?
checkpoint.rubric: One free report per bureau per year.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does applying for a lot of credit in a short time hurt your score?
checkpoint.answer: Each application is recorded on your report, and many applications in a short time signal to lenders that you might be in financial trouble.
checkpoint.rubric: Must mention that applications are recorded or visible, AND that many of them signal risk or desperation to lenders. Reject 'because it looks bad' alone.

segments.title: Tax basics: what SARS takes and gives back
segments.script: If you earn a salary, your employer deducts PAYE, pay as you earn, every month and sends it to SARS. That is an estimate of your annual tax, spread across twelve months. The tax year runs from the first of March to the end of February, and at the end of it you may need to file a return so SARS can check whether you paid the right amount. You do not pay tax on every rand. There is a tax threshold, and below it you owe nothing. Above it, tax works in brackets. The first slice of income is taxed at a low rate, the next slice at a higher rate, and so on. A common misunderstanding is that a raise can push all your income into a higher bracket. It cannot. Only the rand above each bracket line is taxed at the higher rate. So a raise never leaves you with less take-home pay. Now, things that reduce your tax. Retirement annuity and pension contributions are deductible up to a limit, so saving for retirement lowers your bill today. Medical aid gives you a monthly tax credit. And tax-free savings accounts let you save up to a yearly limit with no tax on the interest or growth. This is one of the best deals SARS offers, and most people under thirty have never used one. Filing is done through eFiling or the SARS app. If your employer sent your IRP5 and you have no other income, SARS often auto-assesses you, and you just confirm. If you are owed a refund, it usually arrives within a few days.
keyPoints: PAYE is monthly tax deducted by your employer
Tax works in brackets: only income above each line is taxed higher
Retirement contributions, medical credits and TFSAs reduce tax
Auto-assessment on eFiling or the app if you only have an IRP5
segments.altExplanation: Think of brackets as a staircase, not a lift. Every rand you earn walks up the stairs, and each step charges a bit more than the one below. A raise adds a few rands at the top step. It does not carry the rands on the bottom steps up with it. So no, earning more never means keeping less.
segments.deeper: For the twenty twenty-five tax year the threshold for people under sixty-five is around ninety-five thousand rand a year, and there are seven brackets from eighteen percent up to forty-five percent. The tax-free savings limit is thirty-six thousand rand a year with a lifetime cap of five hundred thousand, and going over the annual limit is penalised at forty percent, so do not overshoot. Retirement contributions are deductible up to twenty-seven and a half percent of income, capped at three hundred and fifty thousand rand a year. Keep your IRP5, medical aid certificate and RA certificate together each year, because if SARS does ask for supporting documents you have twenty-one days to upload them.

checkpoint.prompt: True or false: if a raise pushes you into a higher bracket, all of your income is taxed at the higher rate.
checkpoint.rubric: Only the income above the bracket line is taxed at the higher rate.

checkpoint.prompt: Name one thing that reduces the tax you owe, and say how it works.
checkpoint.answer: Retirement annuity contributions are deductible from your income, so you are taxed on less.
checkpoint.rubric: Must name one of: retirement or pension contributions, medical aid credit, tax-free savings account, AND give a mechanism (deductible, credit, or no tax on growth). Reject answers that only name it with no explanation.
